issues.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected as time-barred when, read as a whole, it alleges facts about discovery of the challenged decision and subsequent steps that prevent the suit from appearing barred on the plaint alone.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that he first learned of the challenged decree when relatives claimed rights under it, but was not then given its particulars.
The plaintiff alleged that the decree’s details became available in a later proceeding, after which he inspected the relevant court file and brought the suit at the earliest possible opportunity.

The application to reject the plaint was made after the written statement, framing of issues and the plaintiff’s cross-examination; limitation was an issue, but no question or suggestion about limitation had been put to the plaintiff in cross-examination.
The trial court rejected the plaint on limitation without considering all its averments, and the High Court affirmed that decision.
issues.conclusion: The plaint was not shown by its statements, read as a whole, to be barred by limitation and should not have been rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d). The orders below were set aside, and the suit was restored for decision on its merits; the Court did not decide the parties’ underlying claims.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court determines whether a suit appears barred by law from the plaint’s averments, not from the defendant’s written statement. The entire plaint must be read as a whole, rather than selecting isolated passages. The applicant must satisfy the court that the plaint does not disclose how the suit is in time. Order VII Rule 12 requires reasons to be recorded when a plaint is rejected. Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provides a three-year period from knowledge for the relevant type of suit. The Court relied on Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, (2003) 1 SCC 557; I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal, (1998) 2 SCC 70; T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, (1977) 4 SCC 467; Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill, (1982) 3 SCC 487; Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, (1998) 7 SCC 184; and Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner, (2004) 3 SCC 137.

rule.if: time_bar_rejection_application and pleading_alleges_later_discovery and pleading_alleges_lack_of_details_at_first_notice and pleading_alleges_follow_up_after_details

predicates.time_bar_rejection_application: A defendant applies to have a plaint rejected on the ground that the suit is time-barred.
predicates.pleading_alleges_later_discovery: The plaintiff alleges that they learned of the challenged decision after it was made.
predicates.pleading_alleges_lack_of_details_at_firs: The plaintiff alleges that the particulars needed to identify or investigate the challenged decision were not provided when they first learned of it.
predicates.pleading_alleges_follow_up_after_details: The plaintiff alleges that, after obtaining the particulars, they took steps to investigate the decision and brought the suit.

issues.definition: When a defendant seeks rejection for a time bar and the plaint alleges later discovery, missing particulars at first notice, and follow-up after obtaining those particulars, the plaint is not rejected as time-barred without further adjudication.
